title: IBM i mental model: objects, libraries and the IFS
outcomes: Describe how an IBM i job finds an object.
Choose the right place for an IBM i object, source member, or stream file.
Explain why a library-list problem can look like a missing-object problem.

sections.heading: Start with the three namespaces
paragraphs: IBM i manages many resources as typed objects. A database file, program, queue, user profile, and job description have an object type and an owner. The type matters: a program name can be the same as a file name because their object types are different.

Libraries group objects in the IBM i object namespace. The integrated file system (IFS) is the path-based file system used for stream files, source archives, logs, and integration payloads. A good developer can move between both views without confusing an IFS path with a library-qualified object name.
bullets: Library object: `APPDATA/CUSTOMER` (object CUSTOMER in library APPDATA).
IFS stream file: `/home/app/import/customer.json` (a path, not a library object).
Object authority is checked before an operation is allowed; a path or name alone never grants access.

command.label: Useful orientation commands
command.code:
DSPLIBL
WRKOBJ OBJ(APPDATA/*ALL) OBJTYPE(*ALL)
DSPLNK OBJ('/home/app')

flow: A user starts a job
The job receives a library list and authority context
IBM i resolves the name to an object or IFS path
Authority and object type are checked
The operation runs or a diagnostic message is recorded

sections.heading: Treat the library list as a search path
paragraphs: For object references resolved through *LIBL, IBM i searches the system portion, product libraries, current library and user portion in that order. Two jobs can resolve the same unqualified name to different objects because their environments differ. Explicitly qualified references and file overrides must also be checked when investigating which object an application uses.

Qualify names in deployment scripts and in high-risk maintenance code. Use the library list for a deliberate application environment, not as a hidden dependency that only works from one developer profile.

command.label: CL setup skeleton
command.code:
PGM
  CHGLIBL LIBL(QGPL QTEMP APPDATA)
  CALL PGM(APPDATA/ORDENTRY)
ENDPGM

sections.heading: Keep source, objects and deployment evidence distinct
paragraphs: A source physical file member is editable source held in a library object. A compiled program or service program is a separate object produced from that source. An IFS stream file is useful for Git checkouts, JSON, certificates, and build artifacts, but it does not replace the compiled object used by a running job.

During a release, record the source version, compiler command, target library, and object authority. That small trail makes a production question answerable: what was built, from which source, and where was it installed?

command.label: Typical build boundary
command.code:
CRTSRCPF FILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) RCDLEN(112)
ADDPFM FILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) MBR(ORDENTRY)
CRTSQLRPGI OBJ(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) SRCFILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) SRCMBR(ORDENTRY)

sections.heading: AS400 basics: follow one customer enquiry through IBM i
paragraphs: If you searched for AS400 programming, AS/400 commands or iSeries development, start by learning the IBM i environment your application runs in. Teams still use those older names in application documentation and job descriptions. In this guide, IBM i identifies the operating-system environment; RPGLE, CL and SQL are ways to write instructions for it. A 5250 screen is one interface to an application. The screen alone does not tell you where its data or business rules live.

Imagine that an operator enters customer 1001 on an enquiry screen. The application calls a program, the program reads a database file, and the job carries the identity and environment used for that work. Your first investigation is therefore a small map: which program, which library, which file, and which job? Write those four answers down before opening source code. A screen label such as Customer Enquiry is not necessarily the compiled program name.

Use object descriptions to confirm the map. A successful display proves you found an object of the requested type in that library. It does not prove that the running screen used that object or that its business data is correct.

command.label: Inspect an example application without running it
command.code:
DSPOBJD OBJ(TESTAPP/CUSTENQ) OBJTYPE(*PGM) DETAIL(*FULL)
DSPOBJD OBJ(TESTDATA/CUSTOMER) OBJTYPE(*FILE) DETAIL(*FULL)
DSPJOB JOB(*) OPTION(*PGMSTK)

sections.heading: Worked library-list example: the right name in the wrong library
paragraphs: Suppose TESTDATA/CUSTOMER contains ten test customers and PRODDATA/CUSTOMER contains live customers. An unqualified native-file reference may find either object depending on the job environment. Looking only at the source name CUSTOMER misses the important part of the problem. Record the resolved library from the job and compare it with the library intended for that test.

The search order includes the system portion, product libraries, the current library and then the user portion. This means placing TESTDATA first in the user portion is not a universal guarantee that it wins every lookup. Check all portions, any file overrides and explicit names in the program. A fully qualified production reference is not redirected just because you changed the library list.

The example below compares the two candidates directly. The expected evidence is two different qualified objects, followed by the failing job’s actual environment. Fix the application startup or test configuration that introduced the mismatch, then repeat the same enquiry. Avoid copying production objects into a random library simply to make the missing-object message disappear.

command.label: Compare candidate objects and the current job environment
command.code:
DSPLIBL
DSPOBJD OBJ(TESTDATA/CUSTOMER) OBJTYPE(*FILE)
DSPOBJD OBJ(PRODDATA/CUSTOMER) OBJTYPE(*FILE)
DSPJOB JOB(*) OPTION(*FILOVR)

sections.heading: Why your QTEMP file disappears in a submitted job
paragraphs: A developer creates a temporary work file, submits an export job, and the export cannot find that file. Both programs say QTEMP/WORKFILE, so the source appears consistent. The missing detail is that each job owns its own QTEMP. The submitted job sees its own library, not the submitting session’s temporary objects. Ending the owning job also removes its QTEMP objects.

Choose the lifetime you actually need. Build the temporary file inside the export job when it is only scratch space. Use an application-controlled persistent staging table with a run identifier when two jobs must exchange records. Give that table an explicit cleanup and access policy. The word temporary in a business requirement does not automatically mean the IBM i library QTEMP.

A useful test uses two separate jobs and records both qualified job names. Create or inspect the work object in the first job, then inspect from the second. The expected difference is the teaching point. Do not use this experiment to conclude that QTEMP is a suitable recovery store for work that must survive job completion.

command.label: Inspect this job’s own temporary library
command.code:
DSPLIB LIB(QTEMP)
DSPJOB JOB(*) OPTION(*STSA)

sections.heading: Read an object name, a source member and an IFS path correctly
paragraphs: A release ticket might mention TESTAPP/ORDENTRY, TESTSRC/QRPGLESRC member ORDENTRY, and /home/dev/orders/ordentry.rpgle. Those are three different references: a compiled object, source inside a source physical file, and a stream file. Decide which one a tool expects before supplying the name. A compiler option for a source member and one for a stream file are not interchangeable.

For a first application inventory, record each program’s object type and library, where its editable source is maintained, and how the build connects them. If the source changed yesterday but the object was last built last month, checking the source alone cannot explain today’s running behaviour. Object timestamps are useful clues; your build record or release commit provides the stronger connection to a source version.

The practical outcome is a short, repeatable handover: another developer can find the object, locate its source, identify the build target and inspect the job that calls it. That is more valuable than memorising a long command list without knowing which namespace each command uses.

command.label: Inspect member-based source and path-based source
command.code:
DSPPFM FILE(TESTSRC/QRPGLESRC) MBR(ORDENTRY)
DSPLNK OBJ('/home/dev/orders/ordentry.rpgle')
DSPOBJD OBJ(TESTAPP/ORDENTRY) OBJTYPE(*PGM) DETAIL(*FULL)

summary: Learn AS400 and IBM i basics with practical examples of objects, library lists, QTEMP, source members and IFS paths, plus a first troubleshooting checklist.
seoTitle: AS400 / IBM i Basics: Libraries, Objects, QTEMP and IFS

title: Data and files: PF, LF, DDS and native I/O
outcomes: Select a keyed read, sequential read, or SQL query for a task.
Explain the relationship between a physical file and a logical view.
Discuss not-found, end-of-file, and record-lock outcomes explicitly.

sections.heading: Model the record before choosing the operation
paragraphs: A physical file stores rows and can have keyed access paths. A logical file describes another view over one or more physical files, often with a different key or selected fields. DDS can define these objects; SQL DDL is another way to describe the database. The choice should follow the existing system and the team’s migration plan.

Before coding, name the record format, key, expected cardinality, and consistency need. That short design note prevents a developer from using a keyed operation where a set-based query or a range read is clearer.
flow: State the business key and expected number of rows
Choose native I/O or SQL based on the access pattern
Define not-found and end-of-file behavior
Define the lock and commitment expectation
Test empty, duplicate, and concurrent cases

sections.heading: Read safely with native RPG operations
paragraphs: CHAIN is a keyed lookup. SETLL positions an access path and READE reads records with an equal key. READ reads the next record in sequence. Every operation needs an explicit status check so stale fields are never treated as a successful read.

For a write, retrieve the intended record, validate the business rule, and update that record. State what happens if another job holds the record lock. A strong interview answer describes the operator-visible message and the retry or conflict path.

code.label: Same keyed lookup in two RPG styles
code.fixed:
FCustomers       IF   E             K DISK
C     customerId    CHAIN     CustomerRec
C                   IF        %FOUND(Customers)
C                   EVAL      greeting = 'Hello ' + %TRIM(name)
C                   ENDIF

sections.heading: DDS and SQL can coexist during modernization
paragraphs: Many IBM i estates contain DDS-described files, SQL-created tables, and logical files that support older programs. Do not remove an access path just because a new SQL statement works in a test. Check which programs depend on record formats, key order, triggers, constraints, and journaling.
A practical migration is incremental: document the current object, add a tested SQL view or index when useful, move one access path, and keep a rollback plan.

command.label: Inspect the object before changing it
command.code:
DSPFD FILE(APPDATA/ORDERS) TYPE(*BASATR)
DSPFFD FILE(APPDATA/ORDERS)
DSPDBR FILE(APPDATA/ORDERS)

sections.heading: Why the correct file can still show the wrong records
paragraphs: An IBM i database file has several identities worth writing down: library, object name, record format and member. A physical file can contain multiple members with the same record layout. Think of the members as separate groups of records inside one described file. If a test expects October records while the program opens the default member, the field definitions can be correct and the business result still wrong.

For example, an import file named INBOUND might contain members SEP26 and OCT26. Check the member list before comparing row counts with a colleague. Also inspect which physical members a logical file member includes; an LF is not automatically a view of every member you intended. The commands below inspect descriptions without changing the data. Record the qualified file and selected member in your test notes so another developer can reproduce the result.
Expected outcome: you can identify the exact source of the records before changing the RPG logic. A matching object name alone is insufficient evidence.

command.label: Inspect the file, members and access path — CL commands
command.code:
DSPFD FILE(TESTDATA/INBOUND) TYPE(*MBRLIST)
DSPFD FILE(TESTDATA/INBOUND) TYPE(*RCDFMT)
DSPFD FILE(TESTDATA/CUSTORD) TYPE(*ACCPTH)

sections.heading: Work through a customer order range with SETLL and READE
paragraphs: Assume CUSTORD is an input-only keyed file whose key is CUSTOMER_ID followed by ORDER_ID. To read all orders for customer 42, supply only the leading customer key. SETLL positions the file; it does not load an order into the record fields. READE then retrieves successive records matching that key. Supplying ORDER_ID alone would not mean “find this order anywhere” because the leading key is still CUSTOMER_ID.

The calculation fragments below assume the file and numeric fields are already declared, customerId is 42, amount comes from the retrieved record, and total can hold the sum. With orders 101 and 102 worth 50 and 75, total becomes 125. If customer 42 has no orders, the first READE sets the end condition and total stays zero.

Keep the search key separate from fields overwritten by a read. Test no matching rows, one row, many rows and the next customer in the access path; that last case catches loops that accidentally use READ instead of READE.

code.label: Input-only customer range: calculation fragments, declarations required
code.fixed:
C                   EVAL      total = 0
     C     customerId    SETLL     CUSTORD
     C     customerId    READE     CUSTORD
     C                   DOW       not %eof(CUSTORD)
     C                   EVAL      total = total + amount
     C     customerId    READE     CUSTORD
     C                   ENDDO

sections.heading: Diagnose a record format level check after a release
paragraphs: A program using externally described native files is compiled with knowledge of the record layout. If a deployed file has a different format level identifier, opening it can fail before your first useful read. A frequent cause is deploying the file change without rebuilding the affected programs, or compiling against one library and running against another.

Imagine a customer code grows from six characters to ten. Inspect the file in the failing job’s actual environment, compare the field definitions with the compile listing, and trace dependent files. Rebuild and test compatible consumers as part of the change. Do not treat LVLCHK(*NO) as a conversion: disabling the check does not make old field positions or lengths understand a new layout.

Expected outcome: the program and resolved file agree on the intended layout. Include both old and new boundary-length data in the regression test. A successful open proves only that one prerequisite passed; it does not prove that every business calculation is correct.

command.label: Read the deployed record definition and dependencies
command.code:
DSPFD FILE(TESTDATA/CUSTOMER) TYPE(*RCDFMT)
DSPFFD FILE(TESTDATA/CUSTOMER)
DSPDBR FILE(TESTDATA/CUSTOMER)

sections.heading: Explain why a logical-file read and SQL return different totals
paragraphs: A logical file can apply select/omit rules as well as a different key order. Suppose OPENORD is an LF over ORDERS that omits closed orders. An RPG loop reading OPENORD and SELECT SUM(AMOUNT) FROM ORDERS are not asking the same question. The SQL reads the base table without the LF’s filter. Copy the business meaning into the SQL predicate deliberately rather than assuming the names describe identical row sets.

For customer 42, use three test orders: OPEN for 50, OPEN for 75 and CLOSED for 90. The open-order result should contain two rows with a total of 125. The unrestricted base-table total is 215. These tiny fixtures make a migration error visible immediately. Check nullable status values and any additional LF select/omit rules before treating the example predicate as equivalent.
An SQL query also needs ORDER BY when the application depends on sequence. An index or logical file existing in the library does not make an unordered SQL result a promised customer/order sequence.

command.label: SQL comparison against the base table — adapt the real LF rules
command.code:
SELECT ORDER_ID, AMOUNT
FROM TESTDATA.ORDERS
WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 42 AND STATUS = 'OPEN'
ORDER BY ORDER_ID;

SELECT COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS OPEN_TOTAL
FROM TESTDATA.ORDERS
WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 42 AND STATUS = 'OPEN';

summary: Learn IBM i physical and logical files, members, keys and RPG file operations through practical examples, level-check diagnosis and SQL comparisons.
seoTitle: IBM i Files Tutorial: PF, LF, DDS, CHAIN and READE

title: Db2 for i: SQL, cursors, commitment and isolation
outcomes: Explain why a set-based query is usually preferable to a row loop.
Build a cursor plan with open, fetch, end-of-data, and close behavior.
Choose a transaction boundary and describe the locks it creates.

sections.heading: Think in sets first
paragraphs: Db2 for i can filter, join, aggregate, and order rows close to the data. Start with the result the business needs, then write the smallest query that returns it. A loop in RPG is still useful when each row drives a side effect, but it should not replace a simple set operation.
Use explicit column lists, meaningful predicates, and a stable ordering when the result is shown to a user. Check the access plan before calling a query slow.

code.label: Readable SQL skeleton
code.free:
select o.customer_id, sum(o.amount) as open_total
  from appdata.orders as o
 where o.status = :status
 group by o.customer_id
 order by o.customer_id;

sections.heading: Use a cursor when the program must visit rows
paragraphs: A cursor has a lifecycle: declare the result, open it, fetch into host variables, handle SQLSTATE 02000, process the row, and close it. Keep the row work small and decide whether the cursor needs a stable snapshot or can see committed changes while it runs.
Never hide SQL errors behind an end-of-data check. Log SQLSTATE and the message text, then choose a retry, rollback, or operator action.

code.label: Embedded SQL control skeleton

flow: Declare a result with a clear predicate
Open the cursor inside the intended transaction
Fetch and validate SQLSTATE
Process one row without doing unbounded work
Close the cursor and commit or roll back

sections.heading: Make commitment and locking a design choice
paragraphs: Commitment control groups changes into a unit that can be committed or rolled back. The boundary should match the business action: one order, one message, or a deliberately sized batch. A transaction that is too large holds locks and journals more work; one that is too small can leave a partial business action.

Isolation controls what a reader can see while other jobs change data. Explain the trade-off in plain language: stronger consistency can mean more waiting, while weaker isolation can expose a moving view. Test the chosen level with two concurrent jobs.

command.label: CL transaction outline
command.code:
STRCMTCTL LCKLVL(*CS) CMTSCOPE(*JOB)
CALL PGM(APPDATA/POSTORDER)
COMMIT
ENDCMTCTL

sections.heading: Keep customers with no orders using LEFT JOIN
paragraphs: Begin a join by stating what one result row represents. If the report needs one row per customer, joining customer, order and payment detail directly can multiply rows and inflate totals. For example, two orders joined to three independent payment rows can produce six combinations. DISTINCT does not repair a total that was calculated over the wrong combinations; aggregate each detail set to the required key first.

This smaller example counts open orders and keeps customers with none. CUSTOMER_ID is unique in CUSTOMERS and ORDER_ID is non-null in ORDERS. Put the open-status condition in ON so it restricts which orders match without removing the customer. COUNT(o.ORDER_ID) counts actual matching orders; COUNT(*) would count the preserved outer-join row even when no order matched.

With customer 42 having two open orders and customer 43 having none, expect counts 2 and 0. Moving o.STATUS into WHERE would remove customer 43. Test that missing-child case explicitly; successful-looking reports often hide it.

command.label: Db2 for i SQL: one result row per customer
command.code:
SELECT c.CUSTOMER_ID, COUNT(o.ORDER_ID) AS OPEN_ORDERS
FROM TESTDATA.CUSTOMERS AS c
LEFT JOIN TESTDATA.ORDERS AS o
  ON o.CUSTOMER_ID = c.CUSTOMER_ID
 AND o.STATUS = 'OPEN'
GROUP BY c.CUSTOMER_ID
ORDER BY c.CUSTOMER_ID;

sections.heading: Make NULL and zero mean different things
paragraphs: NULL represents a missing or unknown value; zero is a known numeric value. If three adjustment rows contain 10, 0 and NULL, COUNT(*) returns 3 while COUNT(AMOUNT) returns 2. Replacing every NULL with zero changes the question, especially for averages: the missing observation should not automatically become a measured zero.

The self-contained query below gives you a small dataset without creating a table. Expect ROWS_SEEN = 3, KNOWN_AMOUNTS = 2 and TOTAL = 10. Use IS NULL to find the missing amount. Do not write AMOUNT = NULL as a missing-value test; use the SQL null predicate.

When a report intentionally displays zero for an empty total, COALESCE can express that output rule. Explain why the replacement is appropriate instead of using it to hide incomplete data. In embedded SQL, a nullable result also needs an appropriate indicator variable unless the expression intentionally supplies a non-null replacement; the host variable alone cannot represent both states.

command.label: Read-only SQL fixture: compare row count with known-value count
command.code:
WITH Adjustments(AMOUNT) AS (
  VALUES DECIMAL(10, 9, 2),
         DECIMAL(0, 9, 2),
         CAST(NULL AS DECIMAL(9, 2))
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ROWS_SEEN,
       COUNT(AMOUNT) AS KNOWN_AMOUNTS,
       SUM(AMOUNT) AS TOTAL
FROM Adjustments;

sections.heading: Use a CTE to show the steps in a business query
paragraphs: A common table expression, introduced by WITH, names an intermediate query result within a statement. CustomerTotals below first groups orders by customer. The outer query then filters those totals. For customer 42 with orders worth 6000 and 5000, the sum is 11000, so that customer appears. Customer 43 with a total of exactly 10000 does not pass the greater-than condition.

This example uses one CTE reference. It is a way to organise SQL, not a CREATE TABLE statement or a persistent object you can query later. A view is a different choice when several statements should reuse a named query definition.

Execution details matter when performance is involved. IBM documents that IBM i 7.5 changed the default handling of shared CTEs referenced multiple times to capture their results for consistency. Avoid a blanket rule that every CTE is always merged or always captured on every release. Inspect the actual plan and release/PTF behavior before tuning a slow report.

command.label: Db2 for i SQL: group first, then filter the customer totals
command.code:
WITH CustomerTotals AS (
  SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, SUM(AMOUNT) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT
  FROM TESTDATA.ORDERS
  GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID
)
SELECT CUSTOMER_ID, TOTAL_AMOUNT
FROM CustomerTotals
WHERE TOTAL_AMOUNT > 10000
ORDER BY TOTAL_AMOUNT DESC, CUSTOMER_ID;

sections.heading: Use a guarded UPDATE and check the affected-row count
paragraphs: Consider a reservation request for three units of item A100. Reading quantity 5 and later writing quantity 2 can lose another job’s change if both jobs read the old value. A conditional UPDATE expresses the change and minimum-stock rule in one statement. This does not replace transaction design, but it avoids a separate unprotected read-modify-write calculation.

The SQLRPGLE fragments assume matching declared host variables and a unique ITEM_ID. A successful update of one row means the reservation applied. Zero affected rows means no row satisfied the predicate; it could be a missing item or insufficient quantity, so choose the user-facing explanation deliberately. More than one affected row indicates the unique-key assumption is wrong. Reject zero or negative requested quantities before executing the statement.

Capture the original SQL status, retrieve diagnostics immediately, and handle errors before relying on the count. If the reservation also creates an order line, put both changes in the same intended transaction and commit only after both succeed. These fragments omit that caller-owned transaction and error-reporting code.

code.label: Embedded SQLRPGLE fragments: host declarations and transaction handling required
code.fixed:
C/EXEC SQL
     C+ UPDATE TESTDATA.STOCK
     C+ SET AVAILABLE = AVAILABLE - :qty
     C+ WHERE ITEM_ID = :itemId AND AVAILABLE >= :qty
     C/END-EXEC
     C                   EVAL      savedState = SQLSTATE
     C/EXEC SQL
     C+ GET DIAGNOSTICS :changed = ROW_COUNT
     C/END-EXEC

summary: Practise Db2 for i SQL joins, NULL handling, common table expressions and guarded updates with worked results, RPGLE host variables and IBM references.
seoTitle: Db2 for i SQL Tutorial: Joins, CTEs, NULLs and Updates

title: RPG development: from opcodes to procedures
outcomes: Read an RPG program as declarations, calculations, I/O, and procedure calls.
Translate a fixed-format operation into modern free-form RPG deliberately.
Explain parameter contracts, indicators, data structures, and test seams.

sections.heading: Read RPG in the order the compiler sees it
paragraphs: Begin with control options and file or data declarations. Then identify entry parameters, procedures, and the main business operation. Finally trace I/O and status checks. This order is more reliable than starting at the first calculation line and guessing what every field means.

RPG opcodes express intent such as CHAIN, SETLL, READE, UPDATE, CALL, and EXSR. Built-in functions such as %FOUND, %EOF, %TRIM, and %SUBST report state or transform values. Say what state each operation changes before explaining syntax.
flow: Declare files, prototypes, and data
Receive parameters and validate input
Read or query the required records
Apply business rules in a procedure
Write results and return a clear status

sections.heading: Fixed format and fully free format carry the same intent
paragraphs: Fixed-format RPG is common in maintenance code because its columns carry meaning. Fully free RPG makes declarations and operations easier to review in new work. The important interview skill is preserving behavior while making status handling and data scope clearer.
Keep examples small enough to test. A keyed read should show the found check, and a write should show the validation and error path.

code.label: One behavior, two source styles
code.fixed:
C     orderId       CHAIN     OrderRec
C                   IF        %FOUND(Orders)
C                   EVAL      status = 'READY'
C                   UPDATE    OrderRec
C                   ENDIF

sections.heading: Use procedures as contracts
paragraphs: A procedure should have a clear purpose, typed parameters, and a predictable result. Put conversion, validation, and database access behind small procedures so a test can exercise them without running an entire display program.
For subfiles and display files, keep screen flow separate from data retrieval. The UI procedure can request a page of rows; a data procedure can own the key range and status rules.

code.label: Procedure skeleton

sections.heading: Choose decimal precision before calculating an invoice
paragraphs: An RPG declaration describes the values a variable can hold. PACKED(9:2) provides nine decimal digits in total, with two after the decimal point. That leaves seven digits before it. This matters when a small unit price is multiplied by a large quantity, or when a total accumulates many lines. A field that displays today’s examples can still overflow at the business maximum.

The fragments below start with an exact decimal value of 12.345 and place it in a two-decimal result. Ordinary assignment drops the extra fractional digit here, giving 12.34. EVAL(H) applies half adjustment, giving 12.35. The point is to make the rounding policy visible, not to round every intermediate calculation automatically.

For an invoice, agree whether the business rounds each line or the final sum; the results can differ. Test positive and negative adjustments, zero, a half-cent boundary and the largest permitted amount. Keep money in an appropriate decimal representation and reserve formatted text for the display or export boundary.

code.label: Decimal declaration and calculation fragments in both RPG styles
code.fixed:
Draw              S              7P3  INZ(12.345)
     Damount           S              9P2  INZ(0)
     C                   EVAL      amount = raw
     C                   EVAL(H)   amount = raw

sections.heading: Use SORTA and %LOOKUP only on populated array elements
paragraphs: An array’s capacity and its business row count are different. You may allocate one hundred elements while receiving only three values. Sorting every allocated element can move unused zero or blank entries ahead of real data. Track the populated count, validate it against the capacity, and use the same range for sorting, searching and processing.

In the calculation fragments below, nums has capacity 5 and the first three entries are 30, 10 and 20. The remaining slots are unused. Sorting the populated portion produces 10, 20, 30. Looking up 20 returns index 2; searching for 99 returns 0. Check the returned index before accessing nums(pos), because element zero is not a valid match.

Sorting is not required for every basic equality lookup. Ordered-array declarations and other lookup variants carry additional requirements. Also avoid sorting customer numbers independently from a parallel array of customer names: the relationship would be lost. Use a record-like data structure when several values belong together.

code.label: Array calculation fragments: declare nums, used and pos first
code.fixed:
C                   EVAL      used = 3
     C                   EVAL      nums(1) = 30
     C                   EVAL      nums(2) = 10
     C                   EVAL      nums(3) = 20
     C                   IF        used > 0 and used <= %elem(nums)
     C                   SORTA(A)  %subarr(nums:1:used)
     C                   EVAL      pos = %lookup(20:nums:1:used)
     C                   ENDIF

sections.heading: Validate an incoming date before using it
paragraphs: A ten-character field containing 2026-02-30 looks like a date but does not identify a real calendar day. Treat incoming screen, CSV and API values as text until validation succeeds. An explicit format also avoids depending on the job’s date format when interpreting an integration payload.

The fragments convert ISO-formatted text inside a small MONITOR block. Declare rawDate as CHAR(10), orderDate as DATE and validDate as an indicator before using them. For 2026-02-28, conversion succeeds and validDate stays on. For 2026-02-30, the error path turns it off. The caller must check the flag before reading orderDate; a failed assignment does not establish a valid replacement value.

Keep this monitor narrow so a later file or calculation failure is not mislabeled “invalid date.” Report the offending input and expected format to the caller. Test a leap-day input, blank text, wrong separators and an impossible day. If a blank means “not supplied,” handle that business case separately from a malformed date.

code.label: Date-validation calculation fragments — declarations required
code.fixed:
C                   EVAL      validDate = *on
     C                   MONITOR
     C                   EVAL      orderDate = %date(rawDate:*iso)
     C                   ON-ERROR
     C                   EVAL      validDate = *off
     C                   ENDMON

sections.heading: Make procedure parameters explain who can change the data
paragraphs: A prototype is a contract between an RPG caller and a procedure. It describes the return type, parameter types and passing rules. A matching procedure interface describes the implementation side. CONST marks a read-only reference parameter: the procedure must not change it through that parameter. An ordinary reference parameter can be used to return a changed value, so its purpose needs to be clear at the call site.

The prototype below describes calculateTax: it receives a decimal amount and returns a decimal tax value. It is a declaration fragment, not an implementation. In a real example, the procedure interface must match and the body must apply the agreed tax and rounding rules. Keep the shared prototype in a controlled copy member so callers do not maintain divergent definitions.

Use small tests with known amounts to verify the contract before connecting screens or files. A useful test also confirms that the input value is unchanged after the call. When parameter size or meaning must change, review every caller; an unchanged procedure name does not make incompatible interfaces safe.

code.label: Prototype declaration fragments — implementation and matching PI required

summary: Learn RPGLE variables, decimal calculations, arrays, date validation and procedure parameters with fixed-format and fully free examples and test cases.
seoTitle: RPGLE Tutorial: Variables, Arrays, Dates and Procedures

sources.title: IBM: CONST and read-only reference parameters

title: Jobs, CL and batch work management
outcomes: Trace a job from submission to a subsystem and job queue.
Use CL as an orchestrator with clear message handling.
Design a batch run that can be monitored and restarted.

sections.heading: A job is the runtime boundary
paragraphs: A job carries identity, library lists, environment values, routing data, and a job log. Interactive and batch jobs can call the same program but have different response and monitoring expectations. A job queue holds work until a subsystem has an available activity level.
When a program behaves differently in batch, compare the job attributes and library list before changing code. The diagnostic message often tells you which resolution or authority assumption failed.
flow: Submit or start a job
Job enters a job queue or is routed directly
A subsystem selects the job for an activity level
The program runs with its job context
Messages and completion status go to the job log

command.label: Observe the work-management path
command.code:
WRKACTJOB SBS(QBATCH)
WRKJOBQ JOBQ(APPDATA/BATCHQ)
DSPJOB JOB(*) OPTION(*JOBLOG)
DSPJOBLOG JOB(*)

sections.heading: Let CL coordinate and report
paragraphs: CLLE is a good boundary for setting the library list, creating temporary objects, calling programs in order, and reacting to expected messages. Keep business rules in RPG or SQL, where they can be tested with data. Use MONMSG narrowly and preserve the original message information.
An operator should be able to tell whether a failure is retryable, data-related, or a configuration problem. Send a useful diagnostic or escape message instead of allowing a silent fall-through.

code.label: CLLE orchestration skeleton
code.free:
PGM PARM(&RUNID)
  DCL VAR(&RUNID) TYPE(*CHAR) LEN(20)
  MONMSG MSGID(CPF0000) EXEC(GOTO CMDLBL(ERROR))
  CALL PGM(APPDATA/LOADORDERS) PARM(&RUNID)
  CALL PGM(APPDATA/POSTORDERS) PARM(&RUNID)
  RETURN
ERROR:
  SNDPGMMSG MSGID(CPF9898) MSGF(QCPFMSG) +
    MSGDTA('Batch run failed; inspect the job log for the original error.') +
    MSGTYPE(*ESCAPE)
ENDPGM

sections.heading: Make batch processing restartable
paragraphs: A restartable batch design has deterministic selection, a status or work table, an operation identifier, and a defined commit boundary. Mark a row complete only after the business effect succeeds. Reconcile the small failure window where the business effect succeeds but the status update does not.
Schedule the job with an owner, expected duration, alert rule, and operator runbook. A schedule entry without a recovery plan is only a timer.

command.label: Example test schedule and inspection; replace all sample objects
command.code:
ADDJOBSCDE JOB(NIGHTLY) CMD(CALL PGM(TESTAPP/NIGHTLY)) +
  FRQ(*WEEKLY) SCDDATE(*NONE) SCDDAY(*MON) SCDTIME(220000) +
  JOBQ(TESTAPP/BATCHQ) JOBD(TESTAPP/BATCHJOB)
WRKJOBSCDE
/* Use the actual number/user/name of a submitted run. */
WRKJOB JOB(123456/APPUSER/NIGHTLY)

sections.heading: SBMJOB succeeded, but did the batch program run?
paragraphs: An operator submits an invoice export and receives a successful submission message. That confirms the request was accepted; it is not the export result. The job may still be queued, may start later, or may fail after startup. Record the qualified job identifier returned by the submission and track that exact run. A job name such as EXPORT can be reused many times, so the job number and user are important.

The example explicitly identifies a program, job queue and initial user library list. Replace those sample objects with your application’s agreed test environment. Once submitted, inspect the queue and then the identified job. If a job is waiting, determine whether the queue is held, attached to an active subsystem and eligible for an available activity slot. Resubmitting immediately can create two exports when capacity becomes available.

Finish the investigation by checking the application’s completion evidence: exported row count, output filename and run status. A normal job end with zero rows can still be wrong when the business expected five thousand records.

command.label: Submit one test run, then inspect the queue
command.code:
SBMJOB CMD(CALL PGM(TESTAPP/EXPORT)) JOB(EXPORT) +
  JOBQ(TESTAPP/BATCHQ) INLLIBL(QTEMP TESTAPP TESTDATA)
WRKJOBQ JOBQ(TESTAPP/BATCHQ)
/* Replace with the job identifier returned by submission. */
WRKJOB JOB(123456/APPUSER/EXPORT)

sections.heading: Works interactively, fails in batch: compare the environment
paragraphs: A CL program calls an RPG program successfully from your terminal but fails in the nightly run. Recompiling the program first adds noise. Build a two-column comparison of the successful interactive job and failed batch job: user, current library, user library list, file overrides, parameters and job description. Also check whether the program expects a display or other resource that is unavailable in its batch use.

SBMJOB can take the initial user library list from the submitting context, from a job description or from an explicit list. Therefore a test launched from your customised development session may inherit conveniences that the scheduler never has. A job description documents intended settings, but inspect the actual active job because application startup code may change them.

Reproduce under the same restricted application identity and startup path using a small test dataset. A convincing correction works without your private library list and does not require the operator to sign on as the program owner. Record the differing setting and its source so the next deployment does not recreate the problem.

command.label: Inspect a specific active job’s context
command.code:
DSPJOB JOB(123456/APPUSER/EXPORT) OPTION(*LIBL)
DSPJOB JOB(123456/APPUSER/EXPORT) OPTION(*FILOVR)
DSPJOBD JOBD(TESTAPP/BATCHJOB)

sections.heading: Read a job log from the cause to the final failure
paragraphs: A final escape message often says that a program ended, while an earlier diagnostic explains the missing object, conversion failure or authority problem. Read the messages around the failure as a sequence. Capture the exact message identifier, replacement values and second-level text. The same identifier with a different library or record key may describe a different incident.

For an active job, display its log and call stack. For an ended job, locate its job log through the available job-log or spooled-file displays; QPJOBLOG is the common spooled job-log name. Do not assume that inspecting your own current job shows the batch failure. Logging configuration also affects how much detail is retained.

A job in message wait needs a deliberate response to its inquiry. Read the valid reply choices and assess what the application has already changed before replying. Record the chosen reply and why. Restarting, cancelling or answering a retry option can each have different business effects; the job status alone cannot choose among them.

command.label: Inspect messages and the call stack for the failing run
command.code:
DSPJOBLOG JOB(123456/APPUSER/EXPORT)
DSPJOB JOB(123456/APPUSER/EXPORT) OPTION(*PGMSTK)
WRKJOBLOG

sections.heading: Test a scheduled batch with a small reconciliation checklist
paragraphs: Scheduling controls when work is submitted, not a promise of when it starts or finishes. For a nightly import, record the scheduled time, submission time, start time and completion time separately. If submission is timely but start is late, investigate queue capacity. If start is timely but completion is late, investigate the program and its dependencies.

Before enabling the schedule, test three input cases: no eligible records, one valid record and one intentionally invalid record in test data. Decide whether an invalid record stops the complete run or is reported while other records continue. The completion message and status table should make that policy visible.

Reconcile attempted, completed and rejected counts after each test. Then simulate a restart after a completed business operation and verify it is not posted twice. Keep the original operation identifier during that retry. A new timestamp-based identifier for every attempt can hide duplicate work. These checks turn a successful scheduler entry into evidence that the business process can run unattended.

command.label: Read existing schedules before adding another one
command.code:
WRKJOBSCDE
WRKJOBQ JOBQ(TESTAPP/BATCHQ)
WRKACTJOB SBS(QBATCH)

summary: Troubleshoot IBM i batch jobs with SBMJOB, job queues, MSGW, job logs and CL examples. Learn to separate submission, execution and business completion.
seoTitle: IBM i Batch Jobs: SBMJOB, Job Queues, CL and Job Logs

title: Modern RPGLE: modules, service programs & runtime
outcomes: Trace a modern RPGLE request from source member to an active ILE program.
Differentiate modules, service programs, binding directories, and runnable programs.
Choose a compatibility and activation-group strategy that makes resource lifetime explicit.

sections.heading: How the ILE pieces connect
paragraphs: Modern RPGLE usually means fully free source, procedures with clear prototypes, and ILE objects assembled for reuse. The important distinction is between the build-time path and the run-time path: a binding directory helps the binder find providers while an activation group owns the resources used after a program is called.

A simple order application might call an *PGM named ORDENTRY. ORDENTRY uses procedures from an *SRVPGM named ORDERAPI. ORDERAPI is made from one or more *MODULE objects. A *BNDDIR can list ORDERAPI so builders do not repeat every dependency on each create command. At run time, the program and service program activate in a chosen activation group.
bullets: *MODULE: compiled code that is not called directly.
*SRVPGM: a reusable, reference-bound package of exported procedures.
*BNDDIR: a build-time list of possible modules and service programs; it holds no executable code.
*PGM: the runnable entry object that a job calls.
Activation group: the run-time boundary for static storage, open files, cursors, and other scoped resources.
flow: Write RPGLE source and define the procedure contract
Compile each source unit into a *MODULE
Package shared procedures in a *SRVPGM and publish deliberate exports
Use a *BNDDIR at build time to resolve only the imports that are needed
Create the runnable *PGM that calls the procedure
At run time, an activation group initializes and owns the program resources

sections.heading: Build a small service, not a giant program
paragraphs: An ILE module is a compiled unit that can be bound into a program or service program. A program is a callable runnable object. A service program exposes reusable exported procedures and data through a binding contract. This separation lets a team change one implementation module and rebuild the affected object without copying the implementation into every caller.

Start an interface discussion with the procedure prototype, parameter types, error contract, and ownership of resources. The object names matter, but the contract is what protects callers. Keep a service program focused: validation, tax calculation, or customer lookup are clearer shared services than one catch-all application library.

command.label: Compile a module, then bind the caller
command.code:
CRTRPGMOD MODULE(APPDATA/ORDERMOD) SRCFILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) SRCMBR(ORDERMOD)
CRTRPGMOD MODULE(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) SRCFILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) SRCMBR(ORDENTRY)
CRTPGM PGM(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) MODULE(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) BNDSRVPGM(APPDATA/ORDERAPI)

sections.heading: Use a binding directory to reduce build noise
paragraphs: A binding directory is an optional convenience for the binding step. It lists modules and service programs the binder may inspect when an import remains unresolved. It is not a run-time registry, a deployment tool, or a way to load code dynamically.

Keep a directory focused on a logical API set. A very large, global binding directory makes builds harder to reason about and can make binding slower. Prefer a small application directory such as APPBND with the service programs the application is designed to use.

command.label: Create and use an application binding directory
command.code:
CRTBNDDIR BNDDIR(APPDATA/APPBND)
ADDBNDDIRE BNDDIR(APPDATA/APPBND) OBJ((APPDATA/ORDERAPI *SRVPGM))
CRTPGM PGM(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) MODULE(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) BNDDIR(APPDATA/APPBND)

sections.heading: Treat binding signatures as compatibility promises
paragraphs: A service program’s binder language describes exported procedures and a signature. When a caller binds to a signature, changing parameter order or type can break the contract. Add a new export for an intentional interface change and keep older exports while callers migrate. Avoid EXPORT(*ALL) for a stable API: it accidentally makes internal procedures part of the public contract.

A good answer distinguishes compile-time binding from run-time lookup and explains how the team detects an incompatible service program before production. Replacing a module alone does not refresh a program that has copied it during static binding; rebuild or update the bound consumer through a controlled release.

code.label: Binder language outline
code.free:
STRPGMEXP PGMLVL(*CURRENT) SIGNATURE('ORDERAPI V2')
  EXPORT SYMBOL('postOrder')
  EXPORT SYMBOL('cancelOrder')
ENDPGMEXP
/* Keep prior signatures when compatibility is required. */

sections.heading: Activation groups define lifetime and cleanup
paragraphs: An activation group is the runtime scope for static storage, open files, SQL cursors, and resources used by ILE programs. *NEW, *CALLER, and named activation groups have different reuse and cleanup behavior. Choose deliberately: reuse can preserve state and reduce setup, while a fresh group can isolate state and simplify cleanup.

*CALLER is often suitable for a cooperating service that should share the caller's scope. A named group can keep a complete application alive across calls when its state and cleanup are managed deliberately. *NEW gives a separate fresh group. When an issue appears, ask which object opened the resource, which group owns it, and what happens on return or reclaim. Do not fix a leak by changing the group attribute without understanding the lifecycle.

command.label: Inspect compiled attributes
command.code:
DSPPGM PGM(APPDATA/ORDENTRY)
DSPSRVPGM SRVPGM(APPDATA/ORDERAPI)
WRKOBJ OBJ(APPDATA/*ALL) OBJTYPE(*PGM)

sections.heading: Build and call a reusable tax service in a test library
paragraphs: Use one small feature to understand the build chain. TAXMOD contains an exported calculateTax procedure and no independent business entry point. TAXAPI is the service program that publishes that procedure. TAXTEST is a separate program whose prototype matches the service and whose job is to call it with known inputs. The library TRAINING and the source members below are prerequisites, not objects these commands create automatically.

First compile the implementation module. Then create TAXAPI using binder source that deliberately exports calculateTax. Compile TAXTEST and bind it to TAXAPI. A caller import must match the exported symbol, including its defined spelling; do not guess the binder name from a mixed-case source label. Inspect the module’s exports and use that spelling in the binder member.

Expected outcome: a test program can call the shared calculation without copying the implementation source into the caller. Compiling TAXMOD again does not by itself replace the copy already bound inside TAXAPI. A release must rebuild or update the containing service program and verify its callers.

command.label: CL build outline — existing test source and binder members required
command.code:
CRTRPGMOD MODULE(TRAINING/TAXMOD) SRCFILE(TRAINING/QRPGLESRC) SRCMBR(TAXMOD)
CRTSRVPGM SRVPGM(TRAINING/TAXAPI) MODULE(TRAINING/TAXMOD) EXPORT(*SRCFILE) SRCFILE(TRAINING/QSRVSRC) SRCMBR(TAXAPI) ACTGRP(*CALLER)
CRTRPGMOD MODULE(TRAINING/TAXTEST) SRCFILE(TRAINING/QRPGLESRC) SRCMBR(TAXTEST)
CRTPGM PGM(TRAINING/TAXTEST) MODULE(TRAINING/TAXTEST) BNDSRVPGM(TRAINING/TAXAPI) ACTGRP(*NEW)

sections.heading: Evolve a service-program interface without misleading callers
paragraphs: Suppose version one publishes calculateTax(amount), and a new requirement needs a country code. Changing the existing parameter list while keeping the old name can break a caller that still passes one argument. A generated binder signature is based on exported names and order; it does not validate the RPG parameter definitions. Therefore a signature that still matches is not proof that the procedure contract remains compatible.

A practical design is to preserve the existing procedure’s behavior and add calculateTaxForCountry with a new prototype. Maintain export order and the required previous signatures in binder source according to the chosen versioning approach. Exercise an old caller and a newly built caller against the replacement service before promotion. Do not remove an old export merely because no new source uses it; an existing bound object may still depend on it.

If compatibility cannot be preserved, make the incompatibility intentional and rebuild the affected consumers together. Record the service version and caller build in the release evidence so a rollback restores a compatible set.

command.label: Inspect the published interface before and after the change
command.code:
DSPSRVPGM SRVPGM(TRAINING/TAXAPI) DETAIL(*SIGNATURE *PROCEXP)
DSPPGM PGM(TRAINING/TAXTEST) DETAIL(*SRVPGM)

sections.heading: Reproduce a second-call bug caused by retained state
paragraphs: A common ILE testing trap is calling a program once in a fresh job and concluding its state handling is correct. Static storage belongs to an activation. When that activation is reused, an application can retain values that were intended for only one request. Replacing the source with clearer procedure names does not automatically remove this lifetime issue.

Imagine a lookup service stores the last successful customer name in static storage. Request A finds customer 42. Request B asks for a missing customer and returns without clearing the output. The screen can now show customer 42’s name for request B. Fix the output contract: initialise request-specific results, return found/not-found explicitly, and let the caller use data only for a successful result.

Run A then B in the same job and same intended activation group, repeat B, and compare with a fresh job. Also test different customers in succession. Activation groups isolate activations, but they are not a substitute for clean per-request data handling. Reclaiming a group can hide the symptom while leaving the defect in the code. The earlier TAXTEST build uses ACTGRP(*NEW), which creates a fresh group for each call; use a named/reused activation group for this specific lifetime test.
flow: Call with a known customer and verify the returned fields
Call with a missing customer in the same activation
Assert not-found and no usable previous-customer output
Repeat in a fresh job to expose lifetime differences
Fix initialisation and result handling, then repeat both tests

sections.heading: Separate compile, bind and activation failures when troubleshooting
paragraphs: An ILE failure becomes easier to diagnose once you identify the phase. A source compilation error concerns the RPG syntax, declarations, include members or external definitions available to the compiler. An unresolved import during binding concerns the modules and service-program exports available to assemble the object. An activation failure happens later, when the running job must locate required service programs and validate their supported signatures.

For example, a test build might bind successfully to TRAINING/TAXAPI, but a production job might resolve a different deployed service or lack the expected object. Adding random entries to a binding directory does not diagnose the running job. Inspect the failing program’s recorded service dependencies, the available service signatures, the job’s library context and the actual diagnostic message.

Write down the phase, qualified object names and first relevant message before rebuilding. The expected outcome is a specific explanation such as “caller requires a signature this deployed service does not support,” followed by a coordinated deployment fix. Recompiling everything without that evidence can make a mismatch harder to reproduce.
flow: Compile: inspect the source listing and referenced declarations
Bind: inspect unresolved imports and candidate exports
Activate: inspect required service objects and signatures
Run: inspect business status and resource state
Retest the exact failing caller in its real job context

summary: Build an ILE RPGLE service, understand module and binding-directory dependencies, preserve exported interfaces and troubleshoot activation-group state.
seoTitle: ILE RPGLE Guide: Service Programs, Binding and Activation

title: Messaging, data queues, data areas and recovery
outcomes: Select a data queue, data area, or message queue for a communication need.
Explain ordering, waiting, ownership, and failure behavior.
Connect asynchronous work to idempotency, journaling, and operator recovery.

sections.heading: Choose the smallest communication primitive
paragraphs: A data queue is designed for passing entries between jobs, often as a producer-consumer channel. A data area is a small named value used for configuration or coordination. A message queue carries messages for a job, user, or program and supports IBM i message handling semantics.

Do not use a data area as a general-purpose database row, and do not assume a queue is durable business history. Persist the business state separately when replay, audit, or reconciliation is required.
flow: Producer records durable work where recovery is required
Producer sends a notification to the data queue
Consumer receives the notification using a defined wait policy
Consumer applies an idempotent business action
Application records completion or preserves failure for recovery

sections.heading: Make waiting and ownership explicit
paragraphs: A receiver should state whether it waits, how long it waits, and what an empty queue means. A sender should handle a full or unavailable queue. Include a correlation or operation identifier so an operator can trace one notification through the job log and business tables. Use QSNDDTAQ and QRCVDTAQ APIs, or the documented QSYS2 SQL services, for sending and receiving.
For a data area, define who creates it, who can change it, its length and format, and how a deployment updates it. A clear owner prevents hidden configuration changes.

command.label: Create and inspect sample communication objects in a test library
command.code:
CRTDTAQ DTAQ(TESTAPP/ORDERQ) TYPE(*STD) MAXLEN(256) SEQ(*FIFO)
CRTDTAARA DTAARA(TESTAPP/MODE) TYPE(*CHAR) LEN(10) VALUE('TEST')
DSPDTAARA DTAARA(TESTAPP/MODE)

sections.heading: Design the failure path before the happy path
paragraphs: By default, QRCVDTAQ removes an entry when it receives it. An application cannot assume that a database commit later acknowledges that queue entry, or that a database rollback automatically returns it to the queue. If losing a notification would lose business work, store recoverable work separately and use a durable operation identifier.

A worker must cope with both repeated and missing notifications. Record business completion with the database effect in the same transaction where applicable. Add retry limits and an operator review path for invalid work. A useful failure record includes the operation ID, object or table, reason and next safe action.

code.label: Application recovery sketch, not a queue acknowledgement API
code.free:
receive notification with timeout
if no entry: wait again or finish normally
load the durable work item identified by operationId
if already completed: skip duplicate business work
claim pending work using the application concurrency rule
apply database change and completion marker in one transaction
on failure: record the problem and leave work recoverable
periodically reconcile unfinished work, even without a notification

sections.heading: Send an order notification and inspect it with SQL
paragraphs: A useful first data-queue exercise sends an order identifier rather than a complete copy of the order. The consumer can use that identifier to read the current business record. Agree the message shape, maximum length and encoding before writing either side. A producer sending a number as packed bytes and a consumer expecting printable text do not share the same contract.

Create a dedicated test queue with an explicit entry length. The SQL example uses IBM i services available on supported release and PTF levels. The queue and library arguments identify the same object used by the native QSNDDTAQ and QRCVDTAQ APIs. The sample notification includes a format version and an operation identifier so future changes and repeated work are distinguishable.

The receive uses REMOVE => NO to inspect without consuming this test entry. Repeating that inspection may show the same entry again; it is not evidence that the producer sent twice. Use a controlled test consumer to remove it when testing actual processing.

command.label: Create the exercise queue in a test library
command.code: CRTDTAQ DTAQ(TESTAPP/ORDERQ) MAXLEN(256) SEQ(*FIFO)

code.label: Send then inspect one test notification in ACS Run SQL Scripts
code.free:
CALL QSYS2.SEND_DATA_QUEUE(
  MESSAGE_DATA => 'v1|order-1001|operation-42',
  DATA_QUEUE => 'ORDERQ', DATA_QUEUE_LIBRARY => 'TESTAPP');

SELECT MESSAGE_DATA
  FROM TABLE(QSYS2.RECEIVE_DATA_QUEUE(
    DATA_QUEUE => 'ORDERQ', DATA_QUEUE_LIBRARY => 'TESTAPP',
    REMOVE => 'NO', WAIT_TIME => 0));

sections.heading: Queue receive is not a transaction acknowledgement
paragraphs: Consider a consumer that receives order-1001 and crashes before updating its status. QRCVDTAQ normally removes the entry when it receives it. A later database rollback does not mean your application now has a broker-style acknowledgement and redelivery workflow. Treat queue notification and business completion as separate facts; design how unfinished work is found again.

One practical design stores pending work durably in a table and treats the queue as a wake-up signal. The consumer claims the work according to a defined concurrency rule, commits its database effect and completion marker together, and records failures for review. A reconciliation process can find pending work when a notification was lost or never sent. This is an application design, not a promise supplied by the queue API.

Test both failure windows: after notification receipt but before the business commit, and after commit but before the consumer reports success. The first should leave recoverable pending work. The second should not create a second invoice when retried. External effects such as emailing or calling another service need their own duplicate-handling agreement.
flow: Store pending operation with a stable identifier
Send a queue notification
Consumer claims the durable work item
Commit database effect and completion record together
Reconcile pending work and investigate failed attempts

sections.heading: Handle empty queues, retries and poison messages differently
paragraphs: An empty queue after a timed wait is a normal outcome for a worker. With the native receive API, a zero data length identifies the no-entry outcome; with the SQL table function, no matching entry produces no result row. Clear or reset your processing state before the next receive so yesterday’s message buffer cannot be processed again by accident.

A temporary resource conflict may be retryable, while a message with an unknown format version is unlikely to become valid after ten identical attempts. Set an attempt limit and delay policy for recoverable failures. Save the operation ID, attempt count and diagnostic details in a review record for invalid work. Do not continuously remove and immediately re-send the same failing item at maximum speed.

For your test, send one valid notification, one unknown-version notification and then leave the queue empty. Expect one completed operation, one clearly reported rejected operation and an idle consumer. Measure those outcomes separately. Queue ordering alone does not guarantee completion ordering when several workers process entries at different speeds.
bullets: Empty: wait or finish normally according to the worker contract.
Transient failure: retry with a bounded delay and the same operation ID.
Invalid payload: preserve diagnostic evidence for correction and controlled replay.

sections.heading: Data area configuration: read safely and coordinate updates
paragraphs: A ten-character data area can hold an application mode such as TEST or LIVE. A CL wrapper retrieves the value into a compatible variable and validates it before deciding what to do. Do not interpret a blank or unexpected value as permission to proceed with the most powerful mode. The value contract belongs in the deployment and operations documentation.

RTVDTAARA protects the individual retrieval operation, but a sequence that reads a shared counter, adds one and writes it back needs coordination across the whole sequence. Otherwise two jobs can both read 41 and both write 42. Explicit object allocation is one IBM i option for such a multi-command data-area operation; cleanup must release the allocation on both success and error paths. A database sequence or transactional table is often clearer for business identifiers.

A local data area belongs to its job. A named application data area is a different shared object with its own authority. During testing, identify which kind the application actually uses, then verify behaviour for the valid, blank and invalid configuration values.

code.label: CLLE reads and validates a named character data area
code.free:
PGM
  DCL VAR(&MODE) TYPE(*CHAR) LEN(10)
  RTVDTAARA DTAARA(TESTAPP/MODE) RTNVAR(&MODE)
  IF COND(&MODE *NE 'TEST') THEN(DO)
    SNDPGMMSG MSGID(CPF9898) MSGF(QCPFMSG) +
      MSGDTA('This exercise requires MODE=TEST.') +
      MSGTYPE(*ESCAPE)
  ENDDO
  /* Continue the test operation here. */
ENDPGM

summary: Learn IBM i data queues, data areas and message queues with SQL and CL examples, timeout handling, duplicate detection and practical recovery scenarios.
seoTitle: IBM i Data Queues and Data Areas: Examples and Recovery

sources.title: IBM: Data queue API and SQL examples

title: Production engineering: debug, secure, integrate and tune
outcomes: Turn a production symptom into a small set of measurable hypotheses.
Separate object authority, adopted authority, and transport security.
Improve performance by measuring the access path, waits, and job behavior.

sections.heading: Debug from evidence, not guesses
paragraphs: Start with the exact job, timestamp, message ID, input, and last successful step. Read the job log, inspect the call stack, and reproduce with the smallest safe input. For RPG, inspect variables at a breakpoint; for CL, trace the command and monitored message. Preserve the evidence before restarting a job.
A production fix should include a way to prove the symptom is gone: a repeatable test, a metric, a log message, or a reconciliation count.
flow: Capture symptom, job, timestamp, and message ID
Check job log and call stack
Form one hypothesis and inspect its evidence
Reproduce safely or add a targeted diagnostic
Fix, verify, and document the recovery

command.label: Useful investigation commands
command.code:
DSPJOB JOB(123456/USER/BATCH) OPTION(*JOBLOG)
DSPJOBLOG JOB(123456/USER/BATCH)
STRDBG PGM(APPDATA/ORDENTRY)
DSPPFM FILE(APPDATA/QRPGLESRC) MBR(ORDENTRY)

sections.heading: Security is part of the design
paragraphs: Check the object owner, public authority, private authorities, adopted authority, and the profile under which a job runs. A program that works for its owner may fail for a real user. Avoid broad *PUBLIC authority as a convenience; grant the smallest access required and document why an exception exists.

For an API, validate input, protect credentials, use TLS, log a correlation ID without secrets, and define how a timeout or duplicate request is handled. IBM i authority does not replace transport and application controls.

command.label: Inspect authority before changing it
command.code:
DSPOBJAUT OBJ(APPDATA/ORDENTRY) OBJTYPE(*PGM)
DSPLIB LIB(APPDATA)
DSPUSRPRF USRPRF(APPUSER) TYPE(*BASIC)

sections.heading: Tune the bottleneck you can measure
paragraphs: Separate CPU, I/O, lock wait, network, and queue delay. For SQL, inspect the access plan and predicates; for native I/O, inspect the key and access path; for jobs, inspect active-job wait reasons and memory-pool pressure. A new index is useful only when it improves the measured plan without creating unacceptable write cost.
Record before and after timings with the same input and concurrency. Keep the change small enough to roll back and watch the job after deployment.

code.label: Select this test query in ACS and choose Visual Explain
code.free:
SELECT ORDER_ID, AMOUNT
  FROM TESTDATA.ORDERS
 WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 1001
   AND STATUS = 'OPEN';

sections.heading: Debug an RPGLE calculation with a small repeatable case
paragraphs: Suppose an order total is wrong only when quantity is three and the unit price has two decimal positions. Start with that input and the expected arithmetic result. Record the program object, source version, parameter types and actual output. A broad statement such as the calculation is broken gives you no test that can prove a correction.

Use a test build with suitable debug information and place a breakpoint before the calculation. Inspect the input values, then step over the calculation and inspect the result field. Check its precision and decimal positions as well as the expression. A mathematically correct expression can still lose information when assigned to a field that cannot represent the result.

STRDBG starts the debugging environment; it does not run the application for you. UPDPROD(*NO) restricts updates to database files in libraries designated as production, but it is not a complete sandbox for every API, IFS action or external call. Use isolated test data and test integrations. Repeat the original case plus zero, negative and boundary values appropriate to the business rule.

command.label: Start and finish a controlled debug session

sections.heading: Authority failure: explain why the developer succeeds
paragraphs: A program works for the developer but the support profile receives an authority error. First capture the failing operation and the exact qualified object. The user may be able to call the program while lacking access to a file it opens later. Seeing a menu or finding an object is not proof that every requested operation is authorised.

Inspect the library and object authorities, the active profile and relevant group memberships. If adopted authority is part of the application design, check the program attributes and call path too. Copying a test program under a different owner can change that context. Avoid making *PUBLIC powerful merely because it removes the error for one test.

Build an access test with two results: the authorised role succeeds at its required operation, and an unrelated profile is still refused. Ask the security owner to choose the intended authority mechanism, then record that decision in the deployment steps. The fix is complete only when the real application identity works after a normal release, rather than through a one-off grant nobody can explain.

command.label: Collect authority evidence before requesting a change
command.code:
DSPOBJAUT OBJ(TESTDATA) OBJTYPE(*LIB)
DSPOBJAUT OBJ(TESTDATA/ORDERS) OBJTYPE(*FILE)
DSPUSRPRF USRPRF(APPUSER) TYPE(*BASIC)
DSPPGM PGM(TESTAPP/ORDTOTAL) DETAIL(*BASIC)

sections.heading: A slow job may be waiting for a lock rather than using CPU
paragraphs: Two users update the same order. One leaves the record in a long transaction while the other waits. Increasing memory or adding an index does not directly remove that transaction conflict. Capture the waiting job, the object or record identified by the diagnostic, and the job that owns the incompatible lock. Then ask what work the owner is still doing.

WRKOBJLCK displays object-level requests, including locks held and requests waiting. It does not display database record locks. Use the record-lock display for the actual database file when the symptom concerns a row. Confusing these two views can lead to the false conclusion that no lock exists.

In a test environment, reproduce the conflict with two sessions and a known key. Confirm when the second session begins waiting and whether it proceeds after the first commits or rolls back. The lasting change may be a shorter transaction, consistent update order or an application message that explains retry. Ending the owner’s job is an operational decision with recovery consequences, not a diagnostic shortcut.

command.label: Inspect file/object locks and record locks separately
command.code:
WRKOBJLCK OBJ(TESTDATA/ORDERS) OBJTYPE(*FILE)
DSPRCDLCK FILE(TESTDATA/ORDERS) MBR(*FIRST)

sections.heading: Compare an SQL query plan with the business result
paragraphs: For an order enquiry, write down the required result before tuning: open orders for one customer, in order-ID sequence. Measure the query with representative data and record its returned row count. A faster query that omits orders or changes duplicate handling is not an improvement.

Select the statement in ACS Run SQL Scripts and use Visual Explain. Inspect how rows are accessed and filtered, whether sorting is required, and the estimates used by the optimizer. Explain-only information is an estimate; Run and Explain executes the statement. Choose deliberately, especially when analysing data-changing SQL or expensive production queries.

Compare the same statement, parameter values, data volume and concurrency after a proposed index or predicate change. Include write cost and other important workloads in the decision. A single fast run against a warm cache is weak evidence. Save the plan and timings so the next developer can see what improved and under which conditions.

code.label: Standalone enquiry query to inspect in Visual Explain
code.free:
SELECT ORDER_ID, AMOUNT
  FROM TESTDATA.ORDERS
 WHERE CUSTOMER_ID = 1001
   AND STATUS = 'OPEN'
 ORDER BY ORDER_ID;

title: Interview lab: design, troubleshoot and code
outcomes: Structure an answer around constraints, trade-offs, and evidence.
Spot hidden failure windows in common IBM i designs.
Practice code-first explanations in both fixed and free RPG.

sections.heading: Use a repeatable answer frame
paragraphs: For a design question, state the business goal and constraints first. Then name the object or service you would use, show the data and job flow, and explain authority, commitment, monitoring, and recovery. End with one trade-off and one test that would change your decision.

For a troubleshooting question, state the symptom you would measure, the first log or command you would inspect, and the safe mitigation. Interviewers are looking for a controlled investigation, not a list of commands.
flow: Clarify the goal and constraints
Choose the smallest IBM i design that fits
Name failure, authority, and consistency behavior
Describe observability and recovery
Give a test and a measured trade-off

sections.heading: Find the hidden failure window
paragraphs: Tricky questions often hide an assumption: a library list is stable, a queue entry is processed once, a record is unlocked, a service program interface never changes, or a batch job can simply be rerun. Challenge the assumption and offer a safer design with an operator path.
When a requirement is ambiguous, state what you would ask before coding. A short clarifying question can prevent a technically correct answer from solving the wrong problem.

command.label: A compact investigation checklist
command.code:
DSPJOB JOB(*) OPTION(*JOBLOG)
DSPLIBL
DSPOBJAUT OBJ(APPDATA/*ALL) OBJTYPE(*ALL)
WRKACTJOB SBS(*ALL)
DSPJOBQ JOBQ(APPDATA/BATCHQ)

sections.heading: Explain code in both RPG styles
paragraphs: The fixed and fully free examples should express the same business behavior. In an interview, describe the input, lookup, status check, update, and test cases before showing source. Mention what you would add in production: prototypes, error handling, commitment scope, logging, and a concurrency decision.
Keep the code skeleton intentionally small. The goal is to show safe control flow and the questions you would resolve with the team, not to pretend a five-line snippet is a complete application.

code.label: Safe update skeleton
code.fixed:
FProducts        UF   E             K DISK
C     productId    CHAIN     ProductRec
C                   IF        %FOUND(Products) AND newQty >= 0
C                   EVAL      quantity = newQty
C                   UPDATE    ProductRec
C                   ENDIF
